sections.title: How does the Pizza tip calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pizza tip calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports tip percentage in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of people eating, the service and the weather); then you type in the bill, the tip, number of slices and the slices eaten (1st Person).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pizza tip calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

X=number of people eating
Total=(((leave a custom tip? > 0) ? ( bill + (((service > 0) ? ( the larger of (distance + weather + 3, bill × service + distance + weather) ) : ( 0 ))) ) : ( bill + tip )))
Recommended tip=(((service > 0) ? ( the larger of (distance + weather + 3, bill × service + distance + weather) ) : ( 0 )))
Cost per person=((((leave a custom tip? > 0) ? ( bill + (((service > 0) ? ( the larger of (distance + weather + 3, bill × service + distance + weather) ) : ( 0 ))) ) : ( bill + tip ))) ÷ X)
Price per slice=((((leave a custom tip? > 0) ? ( bill + (((service > 0) ? ( the larger of (distance + weather + 3, bill × service + distance + weather) ) : ( 0 ))) ) : ( bill + tip ))) ÷ number of slices)
Person 1 initial=(slices eaten × ((((leave a custom tip? > 0) ? ( bill + (((service > 0) ? ( the larger of (distance + weather + 3, bill × service + distance + weather) ) : ( 0 ))) ) : ( bill + tip ))) ÷ number of slices))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Number of people eating set to 2, Bill = 10, Service set to Good and Is your pizza being delivered? set to No. Working through the relationship above gives Recommended tip = 3, Tip percentage = 30 %, Total = 13 and Cost per person = 7.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Recommended tip = 3, Tip percentage = 30 %, Total = 13 and Cost per person = 7 should be roughly the size you expected from Number of people eating set to 2 and Bill = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pizza tip calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the bill and the tip — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pizza tip calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns tip percentage, derived from the bill and the tip. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pizza tip calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the bill and the tip, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter bill in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Bill opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Recommended tip = 3. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pizza tip calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
